name: Peptide stacks (Wolverine stack)

lead: The Wolverine stack pairs BPC-157, a gastric-derived peptide, with TB-500, a thymosin beta-4 fragment. Users take it to speed recovery from injuries and hard training so they can keep lifting, and looksmaxxing forums sometimes extend peptide stacks to skin, bone or height.

The chain is recovery: faster tissue repair means less downtime, more consistent training and more muscle over time. In animal studies BPC-157 shows tissue-protective effects and promotes blood-vessel growth, and thymosin beta-4 binds actin and promotes cell migration. Human evidence is limited to a few small studies, and none addresses appearance.

paras: Users describe running the pair as a recovery protocol around injuries or heavy training blocks, alongside rehab and normal lifting. Products are sold as research peptides.
No regulator has approved BPC-157; health authorities cite insufficient safety data and a theoretical tumour concern. It is banned by WADA, and grey-market products are unregulated.

angle.text: Users pair BPC-157 with TB-500 to speed tissue repair, cut downtime and keep training consistently for more muscle. Support comes from animal studies and a few small human studies, none on appearance.

lead: A peptide stack is a combination of several research or compounded peptides taken together. The "Wolverine stack" is the name commonly given to BPC-157 combined with TB-500, a synthetic fragment related to thymosin beta-4, which proponents associate with tissue repair and recovery.[1][2] In looksmaxxing forums, "peptide stacks" more broadly can also include growth-hormone secretagogues and copper peptides, discussed for body composition, skin, bone mass or height.[3][4]

BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid peptide first reported by Predrag Sikirić's group in Zagreb in 1993. Wikipedia describes the human evidence as limited, mostly small studies, and says the peptide is not approved by any drug regulator for human use.[1] Thymosin beta-4 is a 44-amino-acid protein studied in cell and animal work and in phase 2 trials for wound healing and eye conditions; TB-500 is described in doping literature as a synthetic version of an active region.[2]
No clinical study has tested the BPC-157 plus TB-500 combination for appearance outcomes.

paras: BPC-157, also called body protection compound 157, is derived from a protein found in gastric juice. Preclinical studies describe cytoprotective, anti-inflammatory and tissue-healing effects, and it promotes blood vessel formation in animals.[1]

Thymosin beta-4 binds actin and is present in many tissues. In cell and animal studies it promoted cell migration, angiogenesis and reduced inflammatory signalling, and in phase 2 trials of topical or ophthalmic forms it was reported to speed repair of skin ulcers and improve dry-eye and corneal conditions.[2]

On looksmax.org, users post proposed stacks and ask for feedback; threads titled "BPC 157 and TB 500 Wolverine stack" and various "peptide stack" requests appear alongside stacks built from CJC-1295, ipamorelin, GHK-Cu and others.[3][4][5] Some posters, including teenagers who say their growth plates or facial sutures are still open, ask whether such stacks can add height or facial bone mass, while other users reply that GH secretagogues release less growth hormone than injected hormone and that copper peptides mainly affect skin.[3]
Reports of this kind are anecdotes. This wiki does not reproduce amounts or sourcing.

Health authorities discourage use of BPC-157 because human safety data are insufficient, and some commentators raise a theoretical concern that angiogenesis-promoting peptides could affect tumour growth.[1] Wikipedia reports that New Zealand and Australia control it as a prescription medicine though it is not actually available that way. It also reports that in October 2026 the US Health Secretary announced that BPC-157 and five other peptides could be supplied by compounding pharmacies despite lacking FDA approval.[1]
WADA has banned BPC-157 since 2022 and bans thymosin beta-4; Australian rugby league and football players were suspended in the 2010s over thymosin beta-4 use.[1][2]

No studies found of the combination. For BPC-157 alone, Wikipedia cites a retrospective study of 12 patients with knee pain, a small intra-articular study in 2021, a 2024 pilot in interstitial cystitis, and a phase I trial whose results were not submitted.[1] Thymosin beta-4 has phase 2 trials for pressure and venous ulcers, epidermolysis bullosa and dry eye.[2] None measured facial appearance, bone mass or height.

lore.intro: Users on looksmax.org discuss peptide stacks as options for recovery, skin, body composition and, among younger posters, height or bone mass.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: BPC-157 plus TB-500 (the 'Wolverine stack') accelerates healing and recovery.
